name: Home Router Security

quiz.text: What was the first sign that something was wrong with Alice's network?

answers.text: Her internet was unusually slow and video calls kept freezing.
She received a warning email from her ISP.
Her router was physically damaged.
Her computer showed a virus alert.

quiz.text: Why were unauthorized devices able to connect to Alice's network?

answers.text: Her WiFi encryption was disabled, making the network completely open.
Her router was broken and needed replacement.
Someone hacked into her ISP's systems.
Her computer had malware that shared the WiFi password.

quiz.text: Why is it important to change the default admin password on your router?

answers.text: Default passwords are publicly documented and easy for attackers to find.
The router won't work until you change it.
It makes the WiFi signal stronger.
Your internet provider requires it.

quiz.text: Which WiFi encryption protocols are considered secure? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: WPA2-Personal
WPA3-Personal
WEP
No encryption (open network)

quiz.text: What should you do if you notice unfamiliar devices on your home network? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: Change your WiFi password immediately.
Enable or verify WiFi encryption is active.
Ignore it - extra devices don't affect security.
Check that your router's admin password is not set to default.

quiz.text: If an attacker gains access to your router admin panel, what could they do? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: Redirect your traffic to malicious websites.
Change DNS settings to intercept your browsing.
Monitor all network activity.
Nothing - the admin panel only shows settings.

steps.name: Working From Home
steps.description: Today started like any other day - a cup of coffee, a few emails to catch up on, and a client report to finalize. But something isn't right with your internet connection.
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

steps.name: Something Feels Off

highlighterTexts: Click Run Speed Test to measure ping, download, and upload against the local node.

steps.description: Pages are taking forever to load, emails are slow to send, and a video call with a colleague kept freezing and dropping. Alice opens an online speed test tool and runs a fresh measurement to see what is happening.
steps.instructions: Open the speed test website, look it over and click Next, then run the test.

steps.name: Connection Problems
steps.note: Unusually high ping and low speeds can indicate network congestion, unauthorized devices using your bandwidth, or even a compromised router. Always investigate unexpected performance drops.

highlighterTexts: A Ping of 347ms - normal is under 30ms. This level of latency makes video calls and real-time work impossible.
A Download speed of 2.1 Mbps - Alice's plan is 100 Mbps. Something is consuming nearly all of her bandwidth.

steps.description:
The results are alarming. Alice's ping is 347ms - it should be under 30ms for a normal connection. Her download speed is just 2.1 Mbps, a fraction of the 100 Mbps she pays for.

Something is seriously wrong with her network.
steps.instructions: Review the speed test results, then click Next to investigate.

steps.name: Quick Check

answers.text: Unauthorized devices are consuming bandwidth on her network
answers.explanation: When unknown devices connect to your network, they share the same bandwidth, dramatically reducing speed for everyone.

answers.text: Her ISP is experiencing a major outage
answers.explanation: An ISP outage would typically cause a complete loss of connectivity, not just reduced speeds. Alice still has a connection, just a very slow one.

answers.text: The speed test website is giving inaccurate results
answers.explanation: Speed test results this far below the plan (2% of 100 Mbps) indicate a real problem, not measurement inaccuracy.

answers.text: Her laptop's WiFi adapter is malfunctioning
answers.explanation: A hardware issue would typically cause intermittent drops, not consistently degraded speeds across all activities.

data.question: Alice's download speed is 2.1 Mbps on a 100 Mbps plan. What is the most likely cause?

steps.instructions: Answer the question.

steps.name: Inspecting the Router
steps.note: Default credentials are printed on a sticker on most routers. While convenient for setup, this also means anyone with physical access can find them.
steps.description: Alice suspects her home router might be the issue. Before accessing the admin panel, she needs the login credentials. Most routers have a sticker on the device with the default username and password.
steps.instructions: Click on the router to check the default credentials on its label.

steps.name: Accessing the Admin Panel
steps.description: Alice found the default credentials: admin / admin. She opens her browser and navigates to 192.168.1.1 - the router's admin panel address.
steps.instructions: Open the router's admin panel.

steps.name: Logging In
steps.description:
The router login page appears. Alice uses the default credentials she found on the router label: admin / admin.

Using default credentials is a major security risk - anyone who knows them can access and reconfigure the router.
steps.instructions: Log in to the router using the default credentials: admin / admin

steps.name: The Dashboard
steps.note: An open WiFi network without encryption means anyone within range can connect without a password. Unauthorized users consume your bandwidth and can potentially intercept your traffic.
steps.description:
Alice is in the router's admin panel. The dashboard immediately reveals several problems:
  • 8 connected devices - Alice only has 3 personal devices
  • Encryption: Disabled - the WiFi network is completely open
  • Firmware v2.1.3 - possibly outdated
Eight connected devices when she only owns three? That explains the slow internet.
steps.instructions: Navigate to Connected Devices, look the list over, then click Next.

steps.name: Unknown Connections

highlighterTexts: These 5 unknown devices are connected to Alice's network without authorization.
Unknown devices consume bandwidth (causing the slow speeds) and can potentially intercept unencrypted traffic on the network.
The fix: enable encryption and change the WiFi password to disconnect all unauthorized users.

steps.description:
The Connected Devices page confirms Alice's suspicion. She can only identify 3 devices as her own:
  • Alice's Laptop (her work machine)
  • Alice's iPhone (her phone)
  • Living Room TV (her smart TV)
The remaining 5 devices are completely unknown - names like "android-7f2a", "DESKTOP-X9K2M", and "unknown" suggest strangers are connected to her network.
steps.instructions: Review the unknown devices, then click Next to begin securing your network.

steps.name: Quick Check

answers.text: Enable WiFi encryption and change the password
answers.explanation: Enabling encryption with a strong password forces all devices to re-authenticate, automatically disconnecting anyone who doesn't know the new password.

answers.text: Unplug the router and plug it back in
answers.explanation: Restarting the router is a temporary fix. Without encryption or a password change, unauthorized devices will simply reconnect within minutes.

answers.text: Call the ISP and ask them to block the devices
answers.explanation: Your ISP manages your internet connection, but home router security is your responsibility. They can't block devices on your local network.

answers.text: Install antivirus software on all connected devices
answers.explanation: Antivirus protects individual devices from malware, but it doesn't prevent unauthorized devices from joining your WiFi network.

data.question: Alice found 5 unknown devices on her network. What is the most effective way to remove them?

steps.instructions: Answer the question.

steps.name: Enabling Encryption
steps.note: WPA3 is the newest standard, but WPA2 is still secure for home use. Never use WEP - it can be cracked in minutes.
steps.description:
First priority: enable WiFi encryption. With encryption disabled, anyone nearby can connect to Alice's network without any password.

Enabling WPA2 encryption will require a password for all future connections and kick off unauthorized devices.
steps.instructions: Navigate to Security settings, toggle encryption on, and save the settings.

steps.name: Changing the WiFi Password
steps.description: Encryption is now on, and it uses the passphrase that was already saved in the router settings: 'password123' - one of the most commonly used passwords. Alice needs to set a strong password to prevent the unauthorized users from reconnecting.
steps.instructions: Navigate to WiFi Settings to change the network password.

steps.name: Setting a Strong Password
steps.note: A strong WiFi password prevents unauthorized access. Use a password manager to generate and store unique passwords for every account, including your home network.
steps.description: Alice replaces the weak WiFi password with a strong, randomly generated one. The SecureVault browser extension creates passwords that mix uppercase, lowercase, numbers, and symbols - far stronger than anything she would invent on her own.
steps.instructions: Use the SecureVault extension (the shield icon in the browser toolbar) to generate a strong password. Enable Numbers and Symbols, then click 'Save to Vault' and submit the form.

steps.name: Changing the Admin Password
steps.description: The WiFi is now secured, but Alice logged in with 'admin/admin' - the factory default. If she doesn't change the admin password, anyone on the network could access the router settings and undo all her changes.
steps.instructions: Navigate to Admin Settings to change the router admin password.

steps.name: Securing Admin Access
steps.note: Use a unique password for your router admin panel. If an attacker gains access, they can control your entire network.
steps.description:
The admin password protects access to all router settings. If an attacker gains access, they can redirect traffic, change DNS settings, or install malicious firmware.

Alice uses SecureVault to generate a unique strong password for the router admin - one she will not reuse anywhere else.
steps.instructions: Use the SecureVault extension to generate a strong password and save it to your vault. Then enter 'admin' as the current password, paste the new password into both the new and confirm fields, and submit.

steps.name: Checking Firmware
steps.description: One last step: firmware updates. Outdated firmware often contains security vulnerabilities that attackers can exploit to compromise routers remotely.
steps.instructions: Navigate to Firmware Update and check for available updates.

steps.name: Installing the Update
steps.note: Always keep router firmware up to date. Manufacturers regularly release patches for security vulnerabilities discovered in their devices.
steps.description: A firmware update (v2.2.0) is available with security patches and bug fixes. Alice installs it to close any known vulnerabilities.
steps.instructions: Click Download & Install to update the firmware.

steps.name: Network Secured

highlighterTexts: Only 3 known devices remain connected - all belonging to Alice.
The unauthorized devices have been disconnected after enabling encryption and changing the WiFi password.

steps.description:
Alice checks the Connected Devices page one more time. With encryption enabled and a strong password set, the unauthorized devices have been disconnected. Only her three legitimate devices remain:
  • Alice's Laptop
  • Alice's iPhone
  • Living Room TV
Her internet speed should return to normal now that the freeloaders are gone.
steps.instructions: Look over the clean device list and click Next, then review the highlights and click Next again.

steps.name: Key Takeaways
steps.description:
Alice's slow internet turned out to be a security issue - unauthorized devices were leeching her bandwidth through an open, unencrypted network. If your internet is unusually slow:
  • Run a speed test to confirm the problem
  • Check your router's connected devices list for unfamiliar entries
  • Verify that WiFi encryption (WPA2/WPA3) is enabled
To secure your home router:
  • Change the default admin password immediately
  • Set a strong, unique WiFi password (12+ characters)
  • Keep firmware updated to patch vulnerabilities
  • Periodically review connected devices for unauthorized access
steps.instructions: Click Next to proceed to the quiz.

description: A home router guards every device on your network, and its default settings are often the weakest part. Learn to change the admin password, review connected devices and remove unknown ones, update firmware, use WPA2 encryption with a strong password, and recognize the warning signs of an intrusion.

actorDescriptions.alice: You are Alice, a consultant at Beacon Consulting Group. You work remotely from your home office.

name: VPN Usage & Safety

quiz.text: Why do companies require VPN connections for accessing internal resources?

answers.text: To make the internet faster for employees.
To encrypt data and ensure secure access from outside the corporate network.
To track how much time employees spend online.
To block access to social media websites.

quiz.text: What does "Your IP: Exposed" mean in the VPN application?

answers.text: Your VPN is connected and working properly.
Your traffic is no longer going through the VPN's encrypted tunnel, so anything not using HTTPS is unprotected.
Your computer has a virus.
You need to restart your computer.

quiz.text: What should you do if your VPN disconnects while working with sensitive data? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: Continue working - the disconnection doesn't matter.
Stop accessing sensitive data immediately.
Reconnect to the VPN before continuing work.
Report frequent disconnections to IT Support.
Wait until the next day to reconnect.

quiz.text: Which of the following are best practices for using a corporate VPN? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: Connect to VPN before accessing internal resources.
Share your VPN credentials with trusted colleagues.
Keep the VPN window visible to notice disconnections.
Verify the 'Protected' status before working with sensitive data.
Disconnect the VPN when not actively using internal resources to save bandwidth.

quiz.text: What does AES-256 encryption indicate about your VPN connection?

answers.text: The connection speed is 256 Mbps.
Your traffic is protected by a strong, widely used encryption standard.
You can connect to 256 different servers.
The VPN has been running for 256 seconds.

quiz.text: When working from home, which resources typically require a VPN connection?

answers.text: Public websites like news or weather.
Internal dashboards, client databases, and financial systems.
Personal email and social media.
Video streaming services.

steps.name: Working from Home
steps.description: It's Monday morning. Today you need to access the company's internal analytics dashboard to review some confidential client reports.
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

steps.name: Accessing Company Resources
steps.description: Alice opens her browser and navigates to the company's internal portal to access the analytics dashboard.
steps.instructions: Open the browser and go to the company's internal portal, look it over, then click Next.

steps.name: Access Blocked
steps.note: Companies protect sensitive internal systems by requiring VPN connections. This ensures that data is encrypted and access is limited to authenticated employees on the corporate network.

highlighterTexts: The portal shows "VPN Required" - without a VPN connection, the login form is completely hidden.
Internal resources are only accessible through the corporate VPN to protect sensitive data.
Alice needs to connect to the VPN first, then return to this page.

steps.description:
Instead of a login page, the portal displays a "VPN Required" error. The company's internal resources are protected and can only be accessed through a secure VPN connection.

Without an active VPN, the portal won't even show the login form - access is completely blocked from outside the corporate network.
steps.instructions: Read the VPN Required message on the portal, then click Next.

steps.name: Email from IT

email.message:
Hi Alice,

As a reminder, all internal company resources require an active VPN connection when working remotely. This includes:
  • Internal dashboards and analytics
  • Client databases
  • Financial systems
  • HR and employee portals
To connect:
  1. Open the VPN application from your taskbar
  2. Click the connect button
  3. Wait for the connection to establish
Important: Always verify the VPN is connected before accessing sensitive data. Look for the green "Connected" status and "Your IP: Protected" indicator.

If your VPN disconnects unexpectedly, stop working with sensitive data immediately and reconnect.

Best regards,
IT Security Team
email.subject: Reminder: VPN Required for Internal Resources

highlighterTexts: IT Security sets the rule: every internal resource needs an active VPN when working remotely, from dashboards to HR portals.
The email says what a protected connection looks like, a green Connected status and a protected IP, so Alice can check it before opening sensitive data.
If the VPN drops, she stops working with sensitive data and reconnects first.

steps.description: Alice checks her email and finds a message from IT Security with instructions on using the corporate VPN.
steps.instructions: Open your email inbox and read the message from IT Security, then click Next.

steps.name: Understanding VPN
steps.note: VPNs encrypt all data between your device and the corporate network. Even if someone intercepts the traffic, they cannot read the encrypted data.
steps.description:
A VPN (Virtual Private Network) creates an encrypted tunnel between your computer and the company's network. This protects your data from interception and ensures secure access to internal resources.

Without a VPN, your internet traffic travels unprotected, making it vulnerable to eavesdropping - especially on home networks that may not be as secure as corporate infrastructure.
steps.instructions: Click Next to connect to the VPN.

steps.name: Opening the VPN Client
steps.description: Alice opens the corporate VPN application to establish a secure connection.
steps.instructions: Open the VPN application from the taskbar.

steps.name: Configuring the VPN
steps.note: A VPN certificate on its own is public information. What authenticates your device is the private key that belongs to it, which stays on the device. Unlike a password, that key cannot be typed into a phishing page, which is why IT installs it during onboarding and it should never leave the laptop.
steps.description:
Before connecting, Alice needs to configure the VPN with her corporate credentials. The VPN client requires a server address, username, password, and a digital certificate to establish a secure connection.

The certificate is a digital file provided by IT that identifies Alice's device to the VPN server. Alice pastes in the certificate IT sent her; the matching private key was installed on her laptop during onboarding. It works like an electronic ID badge - even if someone steals her password, they cannot connect without that private key.
steps.instructions: Enter the VPN configuration details.

steps.name: VPN Connected
steps.note: AES-256 is a strong, widely used encryption standard. When your VPN shows it, the traffic between your device and the company network cannot be read by anyone else on the network.
steps.description:
The VPN is now connected. Notice the changes:
  • The status shows "CONNECTED" in green
  • "Your IP: Protected" indicates encrypted traffic
  • Connection time and data usage are being tracked
  • The AES-256 encryption badge confirms strong security
Alice can now safely access internal company resources.
steps.instructions: Click Next to access the internal portal.

steps.name: VPN Protected Browsing
steps.note: The green VPN shield icon in the address bar is your visual confirmation that the connection is protected. Combined with HTTPS, this means your data has two layers of encryption - the VPN tunnel and the site's own TLS encryption.

highlighterTexts: The green VPN shield confirms your connection is routed through the corporate VPN tunnel.
All data between your computer and the company network is encrypted - even your ISP cannot see what you're accessing.
Always verify this icon is present before working with sensitive internal resources.

steps.description: Alice navigates back to the internal portal. This time, the page loads with a VPN shield icon visible in the browser's address bar - confirming that all traffic to this site is routed through the encrypted VPN tunnel.
steps.instructions: Notice the VPN shield icon in the browser address bar, then click Next.

steps.name: Logging In to the Portal
steps.description: With the VPN connected and the secure tunnel confirmed, the login form is now visible. Alice can safely enter her credentials.
steps.instructions: Log in to the internal portal with your credentials.

steps.name: Working Securely
steps.description:
Alice is now logged into the analytics dashboard and begins reviewing the confidential client reports. The VPN ensures all data transferred between her computer and the company servers is encrypted.

She works for a while, reviewing charts and downloading reports...
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

steps.name: VPN Connection Lost
steps.note: VPN connections can drop without warning. Always keep the VPN window visible or enable notifications so you notice immediately when this happens.
steps.description:
Suddenly, Alice notices something has changed. The VPN application shows a red indicator - the connection has dropped unexpectedly!

This can happen due to network instability, router issues, or ISP problems. When the VPN disconnects, your traffic no longer goes through the company's encrypted tunnel: anything not protected by HTTPS is exposed to the local network, and you may lose access to internal resources.
steps.instructions: Click Next to see the impact.

steps.name: Recognizing the Disconnection
steps.note: If your VPN drops while working with sensitive data, stop immediately. Do not continue accessing confidential information until the connection is restored.
steps.description:
Alice immediately notices the VPN status has changed to disconnected. The indicators show:
  • "Your IP: Exposed" in red
  • The power button shows disconnected state
  • No connection time is being tracked
The dashboard also displays a "VPN Connection Lost" warning overlay, blocking access to sensitive data until the connection is restored.
steps.instructions: Reconnect to the VPN by clicking the power button.

steps.name: Back Online
steps.description:
Alice has successfully reconnected to the VPN. Her connection is secure again and she can safely continue her work. She makes a mental note to keep the VPN window visible in the corner of her screen so she can quickly spot any future disconnections.

Alice completes her work on the analytics dashboard. Before closing for the day, she reviews the VPN best practices she has picked up today:
  • Always connect to VPN before accessing internal resources
  • Verify the "Protected" status before working with sensitive data
  • Keep the VPN window visible to notice disconnections
  • Reconnect immediately if the VPN drops
  • Report frequent disconnections to IT Support
steps.instructions: Click Next to complete the training.

steps.name: Conclusion
steps.description:
Congratulations on completing the VPN Usage & Safety training! You have learned:
  • Why VPNs are required for accessing internal company resources
  • How to connect to the corporate VPN
  • What indicators show your connection is protected
  • How to recognize and respond to VPN disconnections
  • Best practices for maintaining secure remote access
Remember: A VPN is your first line of defense when working remotely. Always verify it's connected before accessing sensitive company data.
steps.instructions: Click Next to proceed to the quiz.

description: Learn why VPNs are essential for remote work security and how to use them properly. This exercise covers connecting to corporate VPN, understanding when VPN is required, recognizing connection drops, and maintaining secure access to company resources from home.
